title: Clock Card Matcher
context: Grade 5, the closing pages, the planets' turning times and the clock-card game. An adult sees a table of times and a card game. What the pages are doing is pulling the chapter together: 1 day is 24 h, long lengths of time are changed by multiplying and dividing, a clock face is read as the time passed after 12 o'clock, and an end time is found and written on the 24-hour clock.

writeup.why: Keep 1 day as 24 h beside the Earth's turn, change long lengths of time a step at a time, match a clock card with the time passed after 12 o'clock, and give an end time on the 24-hour clock.
writeup.look: A day bar with the Earth's turn beside it, a ladder for long lengths of time, sixteen face down cards, a time line with jumps, and a tray of six word cards.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Clock Card Matcher' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at x 64, y 108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the number of pairs matched. It is never a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at x 64, y 202. The day bar fills the top of the area along y 230 from x 90 to x 1000, one whole day long, with the Earth's turn drawn beside it along y 320 as a bar a little shorter. The tray of six word cards, second, minute, hour, a.m., p.m. and calendar, stands along y 420, and each turns over to its meaning. On the second phase the ladder of days, hours and minutes stands at x 90, y 250 with the long length of time in deep blue, labelled Given, and the working is written in ink beside it. On the third phase sixteen cards lie face down in two rows of eight along y 260 and y 470, each 110 by 170. A clock card is a round clock face with twelve numbers, its hour hand and minute hand near-black ink and its hour hand moved on from its number for the minutes. A time card is the time passed after 12 o'clock, in minutes alone or in seconds alone. Two cards are turned at a time, and a pair that matches stays face up in green, labelled Answer. On the fourth phase the time line with the start and the length of time in deep blue runs along y 400, the jumps in violet, labelled Jump, and the end time is written on the 24-hour clock in green, labelled Answer, at x 120, y 650. The row of five can-dos stands at x 850, y 660, and each is ticked as it is met. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at x 1186, y 250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at x 1170, y 368 (388 by 363). The pad is ten number keys with a delete key, and keys for days, h, min and s. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own, and the nine tools of this chapter share them. What the question gives, as a clock time, a length of time, a start date or a number of days, is deep blue, labelled Given or Start. What the working reaches, as an end time, a length of time, a converted time or a date, is green, labelled Answer, End or How long. The thin second hand and the seconds it counts are vermilion, labelled Second hand. One jump along a time line, and one regrouped unit carried or borrowed, are violet, labelled Jump, Carry or Regroup. On a day bar the half from noon until just before midnight is rose, labelled p.m., and the half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside its outline, labelled a.m. The hand, digit, column, jump or date being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open, labelled Place holder, and for nothing else. The hour hand and the minute hand, dials, tick marks, time lines, arrows, operation signs and step labels are near-black ink, and anything dimmed fades to half strength. Chrome never borrows one of the content colours, and each reading survives with the colour taken away, because a part is told by its written label before it is told by its colour.
writeup.finish: The matched pairs stay face up on the stage with the last end time beside them in green, and the row of five can-dos stays as the child ticked it.

writeup.delight: On the third phase, when the last pair is matched, all sixteen cards flip face up together and the eight clock faces tick round to their times one after another.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing yet matched. On the first phase a day bar for 1 day lies across the top with a slightly shorter bar for the Earth's turn beside it, and the tray of six word cards below. On the second the ladder of days, hours and minutes holds a long length of time in deep blue. On the third sixteen cards lie face down in two rows of eight. On the fourth a time line holds a start and a length of time in deep blue with the 24-hour clock waiting beside it. One thing moves, once: the shorter bar, the first card or the time line gives one slow pulse while the voice speaks its opening line.
writeup.freePlay: Any clock card set and matched, any length of time changed on the ladder, and any end time jumped and written on both clocks. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on the Earth's turn, long lengths of time, clock cards and time cards, and an end time on the 24-hour clock.
voiceLines: A day, a ladder of time and sixteen cards face down.
Are the two bars exactly the same? Which one is a little shorter?
One step at a time. Which unit comes next?
Turn two cards. Do the hours and minutes match the time card?
Jump the hours, then the minutes. Now write it on the twenty-four hour clock.
A new round. Play it the same way.
Free play. Turn any cards and set any time.
Look at the cards again. Do the hands and the time agree?
You matched clock cards, changed long lengths of time and wrote an end time.

source_tool.name: Clock Card Matcher
source_tool.blurb: Set the Earth's turn beside a day, change long lengths of time a step at a time, match clock cards with the time passed after 12 o'clock, and write an end time on the 24-hour clock.

serves.exercise: making flashcards for six vocabulary words
ticking the self-assessment list of five can-dos
finding how much less than a day the Earth's turn takes
finding the number of hours in a leap year
turning the hours of a leap year into minutes
adding the turning times of two planets
finding in minutes how much longer one planet's turn is than another's
giving in 24-hour time when a planet's turn ends after a morning start
playing the math lab game of matching clock cards with time cards

source_tool.description: A day bar fills the top of the working area, one whole day long, with the Earth's turn drawn beside it as a slightly shorter bar. Below it, on the second phase, a ladder of days, hours and minutes holds a long length of time in deep blue, labelled Given. On the third phase sixteen cards lie face down in two rows of eight, eight clock cards and eight time cards. A clock card is a round clock face with twelve numbers, its hour hand and minute hand near-black ink and its hour hand moved on from its number for the minutes; a time card is the time passed after 12 o'clock, written in minutes alone or in seconds alone. Two cards are turned at a time and a pair that matches stays face up in green, labelled Answer. On the fourth phase a time line with a start and a length of time set on it in deep blue jumps the whole hours and then the minutes in violet, labelled Jump, and the end time is written on the 24-hour clock in four digits and the word hours. A tray of six word cards, second, minute, hour, a.m., p.m. and calendar, turns over to their meanings, and a row of five can-dos is ticked as each is met. The running count at the top left of the canvas counts the pairs matched.
source_tool.art_direction: Clock cards spread on a classroom carpet / Picture book

modes.freePlay: Out of scope here. It is not reached from inside a phase mount, because a phase mount ends idle and has no finish card to reach it from. writeup.freePlay stays as the record of what that activity is, for whoever builds it as its own thing.

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: round clock faces with twelve numbers and sixty small marks, a day bar from midnight to midnight, a time line with jumps, columns of hours, minutes and seconds, and month calendars with seven columns.

Every clock time is written in one notation: 4:15 p.m. for a 12-hour time, with a colon and a.m. or p.m., and 1615 hours for a 24-hour time, four digits and the word hours, never a colon and never a dot. Noon is written 12 noon and midnight 12 midnight. A length of time is written 2 h 15 min, 3 days 5 h and 40 s, or in words, and never as a clock time.

Every hour hand sits at its true angle: it moves on from each number as the minutes pass, so at a quarter past it has gone a quarter of the way to the next number. The minute hand is long, the hour hand short and thick, and the second hand thin, longer than both and vermilion. Label lines stay outside the dial.
A time line that passes 12 midnight shows midnight as its own mark and says the next day after it. A count of days always says whether both the first and the last day are counted.
Nothing is animated except the one thing being explained: hands turning, a jump along a time line, a carried unit moving to the next column, or dates being counted on a calendar.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a hand, a digit, a jump or a date the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. This chapter colours the roles a time plays in a piece of working: what the question gives, a clock time, a length of time, a start date or a number of days, is deep blue, and what the working reaches, an end time, a length of time, a converted time or a date, is green; those two are the same two in every tool and every picture of this chapter. The thin second hand and the seconds it counts are vermilion. One jump along a time line, and one regrouped unit carried or borrowed, is violet. The half of the day from noon until just before midnight is rose on a day bar, and the half from midnight until just before noon stays warm white inside its outline. The hand, digit, column, jump or date being worked on now is amber. Grey is kept for a zero holding a place open at the front of a 24-hour time. The hour hand and the minute hand are near-black ink. Each role is named in writing first, with the words Given, Answer, Second hand, Jump, Carry, a.m., p.m., Noon and Midnight, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Look at the cards again. Do the hands and the time agree?
voice.onNext: A new round. Play it the same way.
voice.opening: A day, a ladder of time and sixteen cards face down.
voice.onFinish: You matched clock cards, changed long lengths of time and wrote an end time.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Turn any cards and set any time.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.
voice.voicePreference: an English voice, female where one is offered

phase_map.concept: An end time on the 24-hour clock

placement.where: After the class has made paper clock cards and time cards and played the matching game by hand, and has ticked its own can-dos. The tool is what draws every hour hand at its true place and checks a match, which hand-drawn cards cannot.

answer_key.rule: The Earth turns once round in about 23 h 56 min, a little less than a day. 1 day is still 24 h. To change days into hours multiply by 24, and hours into minutes by 60: 2 days 3 h is 51 h, and 51 h is 3060 min. A clock card shows a time of day, and its time card is the time passed after 12 o'clock, in minutes or in seconds: 25 min past 6 is 385 min. Every hour hand moves on for the minutes. An end time is jumped from the start and written on the 24-hour clock: 7 h 40 min after 5:35 a.m. is 1:15 p.m., which is 1315 hours.
answer_key.wrong: The stage keeps the child's cards. A clock card matched with the wrong time card stays beside it, and the time after 12 o'clock that its clock really shows is lit amber. A conversion that stops halfway, such as days changed to hours but not yet to minutes, stays with the missing step lit amber. An end time left on the 12-hour clock when the question asks for the 24-hour clock stays, and the four-digit form is lit amber beside it. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The Earth's turn is not exactly 1 day.
It takes about 23 h 56 min, a little less than a day.
A clock day is 1 day, which is 24 h.
So the Earth's turn is a little shorter than a clock day, and both facts are true.
items.answer: The Earth turns once round in about 23 h 56 min, a little less than a day. A clock still counts 1 day as 24 h.
items.question: A pupil says the Earth turns once round in exactly 1 day. What is the better thing to say?
items.checkpoint: The Earth's turn is a little less than a day, and 1 day is still 24 h.
items.misconception: Making a clock day shorter than 24 h, to match the Earth's turn.

steps: Change to hours first: 2 x 24 = 48, and 48 + 3 = 51, so 2 days 3 h is 51 h.
items.question: How many minutes are there in 2 days 3 h?
items.checkpoint: Change a long length of time a step at a time: multiply by 24 for hours, then by 60 for minutes.
items.misconception: Multiplying the days by 60 straight away, and missing the step through the hours.

steps: From 12 o'clock to 6 o'clock is 6 h, and 6 x 60 = 360, so 6 h is 360 min.
So the time card is 385 min, the time passed after 12 o'clock.
On the card the hour hand has moved on from the 6 for these minutes, so it is just past 6.
items.question: A clock card shows 25 min past 6. Which time card matches it, in minutes after 12 o'clock?

teaching_notes: Keep 1 day as 24 h. The Earth turns once round in about 23 h 56 min, a little less than a day, so a clock day and the Earth's turn are not the same. Change long lengths of time one step at a time, from days to hours to minutes. Match each clock card with the time passed after 12 o'clock, in minutes or in seconds, and draw every hour hand moved on for the minutes. Give an end time on the 24-hour clock as four digits and the word hours. The self-assessment is the child's own: let each can-do be ticked honestly.
